questions.stem: Which set of lights does a power-driven vessel of 80 m show when underway?
options: One masthead light, sidelights and a sternlight
Two masthead lights, after one higher, plus side and stern
Two masthead lights in a vertical line, sidelights and a sternlight
An all-round white light and sidelights
questions.explanation: Rule 23(a) requires a forward masthead light, a second masthead light abaft of and higher than it, sidelights and a sternlight. Only vessels under 50 m may omit the second masthead light. Two masthead lights in a vertical line is a towing or pushing signal, and the all-round white option is for vessels under 12 m.

questions.stem: A 40 m power-driven vessel is underway at night showing one masthead light, sidelights and a sternlight. Is she showing correct lights?
options: Yes, but only if she is in a harbour
Yes: under 50 m a second one is optional
No, every power-driven vessel over 20 m must show two masthead lights
No, she must also show an all-round white light
questions.explanation: Rule 23(a)(ii) says a vessel of less than 50 m is not obliged to show the after masthead light, though she may. The 20 m figure matters for light positions in Annex I, not for whether the second masthead light is required.

questions.stem: At night you see a white masthead light, a red sidelight, and an all-round flashing yellow light. What is she?
options: A vessel being pushed ahead in the Great Lakes Basin
An air-cushion vessel, non-displacement, port side
A tug towing, seen from her port side
A WIG craft taking off from the water
questions.explanation: Rule 23(b) adds an all-round flashing yellow light to the normal power-driven lights of an air-cushion vessel in non-displacement mode. The red sidelight means you see her port side. A tug's towing light is a steady yellow light over the sternlight, a WIG craft adds a high-intensity flashing red light, and the special flashing light on a pushed vessel is a Great Lakes provision shown at the forward end.

questions.stem: Which extra light does a WIG craft show, and when?
options: Two all-round red lights in a vertical line when landing
An all-round flashing yellow light, whenever on the water
A blue flashing light when in flight
A bright flashing red when taking off, landing or flying low
questions.explanation: Rule 23(c) gives a WIG craft a high-intensity all-round flashing red light, only when taking off, landing and in flight near the surface. Flashing yellow is the air-cushion vessel light, blue flashing is the Canadian identification signal, and two reds mean not under command.

questions.stem: What lights may a 10 m power-driven workboat show underway instead of the full masthead light, sidelights and sternlight?
options: An all-round white light and sidelights
An all-round white light only, whatever her speed
Sidelights only
A sternlight and a masthead light
questions.explanation: Rule 23(d)(i) lets a power-driven vessel under 12 m show an all-round white light and sidelights instead. Sidelights alone leave her invisible from astern, and the white-light-only option is limited to slow vessels under 7 m and does not apply to Canadian vessels.

questions.stem: A Canadian 6 m aluminium skiff with a top speed of 6 knots runs at night near Prince Rupert. Under the Canadian Collision Regulations, which statement is correct?
options: She needs no lights because she is under 7 m
Sidelights too: the under-7 m option isn't in Canada
She may show only an all-round white light, because she is under 7 m and slower than 7 knots
She may show only a hand torch when another vessel approaches
questions.explanation: The international Rule 23(d)(ii) allows an all-round white light only for a power-driven vessel under 7 m and 7 knots or less, but the Canadian Rule 23(e) says that option does not apply to Canadian power-driven vessels in any waters. She can use the under-12 m option (all-round white light and sidelights) or the full set. The torch option is for small sailing vessels and vessels under oars.

questions.stem: Under Annex I, on a power-driven vessel of 20 m or more with two masthead lights, how must they be placed relative to each other?
options: The after light at least 2 m lower, and the two at least a quarter of the length apart
The forward light higher, and the two at least 100 m apart on every vessel
Both at the same height, at least 10 m apart
After light 4.5 m+ higher; half the length apart (max 100 m)
questions.explanation: Annex I section 2(a)(ii) puts the after masthead light at least 4.5 m vertically higher than the forward one, and section 3(a) sets a horizontal distance of at least half the vessel's length, never more than 100 m required. The quarter-length and smaller vertical figures are Great Lakes Basin modifications, and the forward light is the lower one.

questions.stem: You are fitting an all-round white light and sidelights to a 9 m power-driven vessel. Under Annex I, how high must the white light be relative to the sidelights?
options: At least 4.5 m higher than the sidelights
There is no height requirement for vessels under 12 m
At least 1 m higher than the sidelights
At the same height as the sidelights
questions.explanation: Annex I section 2(d.1) requires a masthead light or the Rule 23(d)(i) all-round white light carried with sidelights to be at least 1 m higher than the sidelights, and a Canadian modification repeats this for vessels under 12 m in Canadian inland waters. 4.5 m is the masthead separation on larger vessels.
